front: What does a PCIe x16 slot typically host?
back: A discrete GPU / high-bandwidth video card.

front: Is PCIe serial or parallel?
back: Serial. That is why it is faster than older parallel buses like PCI/PATA.

front: M.2 vs NVMe — which is the form factor?
back: M.2 is the form factor. NVMe is the protocol. An M.2 drive can be NVMe or SATA.

front: Rank storage from fastest to slowest (this guide).
back: PCIe → M.2/NVMe → SATA 3 (600 MB/s) → SATA 2 → SATA 1 → PATA.

front: Single-layer Blu-ray capacity?
back: About 25 GB.

front: Single-layer DVD capacity?
back: About 4.7 GB.

front: PSU: wall vs PC current type
back: Wall = AC in. Components need DC out. The PSU converts AC → DC.

front: Standard PC PSU DC rails
back: +3.3V, +5V, +12V, and −12V (rare). Not +4.3V, +8V, or +110V DC.

front: What is a redundant power supply?
back: A backup PSU so the system keeps running if the primary fails — common on servers.

front: Hot-swappable means…
back: You can insert/remove the device without turning system power off (after proper OS handling).

front: RAID 5 minimum disks and method
back: 3 disks. Striping with parity. Survives one disk failure.

front: Best slot for a video card
back: PCIe x16. PCIe x128 is not a real standard. AGP is obsolete.

front: Windows 11 TPM requirement
back: TPM 2.0 is mandatory and often blocks upgrades.

front: Windows 11 RAM and storage minima (this guide)
back: 4 GB RAM (8 GB recommended) and 64 GB storage.

front: Windows Home vs Pro (domain / BitLocker / RDP)
back: Home cannot join a domain, no BitLocker, no RDP host. Pro can.

front: 32-bit to 64-bit Windows
back: Clean install only. No in-place upgrade.

front: Boot sequence in order
back: POST → boot loader → kernel load → logon → shell/desktop.

front: When do you pick NTFS vs exFAT vs FAT32?
back: NTFS internal/Windows security. exFAT USB/cross-platform. FAT32 legacy only (4 GB file cap).

front: HKLM vs HKCU
back: HKLM = machine (hardware, services). HKCU = current user settings.

front: Deny vs Allow NTFS permissions
back: Explicit Deny wins over Allow.

front: Device Manager scope
back: Hardware only — not applications or services. Launch with devmgmt.msc.

front: Event Viewer: System vs Security logs
back: System = OS/drivers/reboots. Security = logons and permission events.

front: Five main registry hives
back: HKLM, HKCU, HKCR, HKEY_USERS, HKEY_CURRENT_CONFIG.

front: MBR vs GPT
back: MBR legacy, 4 primary partitions. GPT modern, UEFI requires GPT.

front: Where is BCD on UEFI?
back: On the ESP (EFI System Partition), not C:\boot.

front: Sleep vs hibernate
back: Sleep keeps RAM powered (fast). Hibernate writes RAM to disk (saves more power).

front: Defrag vs TRIM
back: Defrag HDDs. TRIM SSDs. Do not treat defrag as the SSD fix.

front: Is WinPE a setup pass?
back: No. WinPE is a boot environment. Passes include auditSystem, generalize, auditUser, OOBE.

front: sysprep /generalize does what?
back: Removes hardware-specific drivers and SIDs so the image can run on other PCs.

front: Prepare, capture, deploy tools
back: sysprep prepares. ImageX/DISM captures a .wim. WDS deploys.

front: Correct image workflow order
back: Configure reference PC → sysprep /oobe /generalize /shutdown → WinPE → capture → WDS → PXE → OOBE.

front: Windows 11 Insider on Home?
back: No. Pro, Education, Enterprise only (this guide).

front: Semi-Annual Channel vs LTSC
back: Semi-Annual = regular public releases. LTSC = long-term, few feature changes.

front: bootrec /rebuildbcd vs /fixmbr
back: /rebuildbcd rebuilds BCD (modern/UEFI). /fixmbr repairs the legacy MBR.

front: Windows workstation SMB connection limit
back: 20 concurrent connections.

front: First troubleshooting step
back: Identify the problem — gather symptoms and ask questions before changing the system.

front: Safe Mode with Networking vs minimal
back: Networking adds network drivers so you can download fixes. Minimal is local drivers only.

front: Boot repair order (least to most destructive)
back: Startup Repair → System Restore → bootrec → SFC → Reset this PC → reimage.

front: DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL usually means
back: A bad driver. Roll it back in Safe Mode.

front: tracert vs pathping
back: tracert shows the path. pathping shows the path and measures packet loss.

front: Malware removal order
back: Identify/verify → quarantine → remediate → educate.

front: How often should AV definitions update?
back: Daily, not weekly.

front: SFC vs regedit
back: SFC repairs system files. regedit edits the registry. Wrong tool for file corruption.

front: Unactivated Windows restriction
back: Personalization (wallpaper, etc.). Apps and updates still work.

front: DHCP ports
back: UDP 67 server, UDP 68 client.

front: DORA
back: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge.

front: What is 169.254.x.x?
back: APIPA. DHCP failed. Not a usable routed address.

front: A vs AAAA record
back: A = IPv4. AAAA = IPv6.

front: Can ping IP but not the name
back: DNS problem. Confirm with nslookup.

front: Cannot reach by IP or name
back: Network path / connectivity — not a DNS-only issue.

front: RAID 0 vs RAID 1
back: 0 stripes with no redundancy. 1 mirrors for redundancy.

front: RAID 5 rebuild access (this guide)
back: Cannot access the volume until rebuild finishes.

front: RAID 10 rebuild access (this guide)
back: Can stay online because of mirrored pairs.

front: NAS vs SAN in one line
back: NAS = Ethernet file storage for SMB/home. SAN = high-speed block storage (often Fibre Channel) for enterprise.

front: 3-2-1 backup rule
back: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 offsite. RAID is not a backup.

front: Drill: sysprep command from class
back: sysprep /oobe /generalize /shutdown then capture, then WDS.

front: Memory trick: A vs AAAA
back: One A = IPv4. Four As = IPv6 (bigger).

front: 5 GB file on a USB stick — file system?
back: exFAT or NTFS. FAT32 cannot store files over 4 GB.

front: ipconfig shows 169.254 — next command?
back: ipconfig /release then /renew after checking the DHCP server/cable.

front: Indexing Options vs File Explorer Options
back: Indexing = search catalog. Explorer Options = view/hidden files behavior.

front: Max Ethernet run before attenuation
back: 100 meters (about 328 ft) for any twisted-pair Ethernet.

front: Cat 5e vs Cat 6 vs Cat 6a top speeds
back: 5e = 1 Gb/s (100 m). 6 = 10 Gb/s to 55 m. 6a = 10 Gb/s to 100 m.

front: RJ-45
back: Standard 8P8C connector for Ethernet twisted pair.

front: T568A vs T568B
back: Two 8-wire pinout standards. Both ends must match (straight-through); A on one end + B on other = legacy crossover.

front: Single-mode vs multimode fiber
back: SMF: laser, long haul, 9 micron core. MMF: LED, shorter building runs, 50 or 62.5 micron core.

front: Why fiber beats copper near motors
back: Fiber carries light, so it is immune to EMI and crosstalk.

front: PoE wattages: af / at / bt
Tone generator + probe
back: Traces one cable out of a bundle by sending an audible signal down the wire.

front: Q: Which connectors work with an analog monitor? (choose two)
back: VGA and DVI-A. VGA is the classic analog D-sub; DVI-A is the analog-only DVI variant. HDMI/DisplayPort/DVI-D are digital.

front: Q: USB 2.0 (High Speed) maximum speed?
back: 480 Mbps. (USB 1.1 = 12 Mbps, USB 3.0 = 5 Gbps, USB 3.1 = 10 Gbps, USB4 = 40 Gbps.)

front: Q: What does a YELLOW USB port mean?
back: Always-on charging — it can charge devices even when the PC is powered off. Blue = USB 3.x. Color shows function, not version.

front: Q: Which interface equals DisplayPort + PCIe?
back: Thunderbolt. Thunderbolt 2 = oval mini-DisplayPort connector; Thunderbolt 3/4 = USB-C.

front: Q: Which two standards share the same USB-C connector?
back: Thunderbolt 3 and USB4.

front: Q: eSATA maximum throughput — and does it supply power?
back: 6 Gbps, and NO — eSATA carries data only, no power. It's also slower than USB4/TB3 (40 Gbps).

front: Q: Which power connector for PATA drives and DVD-ROMs?
back: Molex (legacy 4-pin, power only). Modern SATA drives use the SATA power connector.

front: Q: What signal does VGA use?
back: ANALOG. HDMI and DisplayPort are digital; DVI can be analog (DVI-A), digital (DVI-D), or both (DVI-I).

front: Hub (aka repeater) — how does it forward traffic?
back: Repeats every frame received on one port out of ALL other ports. One big collision domain; inefficient and insecure.

front: Switch — why can it send one-to-one (unicast)?
back: It has an ASIC chip with programming that builds a MAC address table (CAM table) mapping MAC+IP to each port; each port is its own collision domain.

front: Router — what does it forward on, and what does it block?
back: Forwards based on IP addresses and routing tables (route print). It does NOT forward broadcasts — every router interface is a broadcast domain boundary.

front: MAC address: length, format, changeable?
back: 48-bit hexadecimal (0-9, A-F), burned into the NIC permanently. Spoofing only changes it in memory. First half = OUI (manufacturer), second half = serial.

front: What does OUI stand for?
back: Organizational Unique Identifier — the first half of a MAC address identifying the manufacturer (e.g., Intel). Exam expects you to know it cold.

front: What is ARP and what does it do?
back: ARP resolves a local IPv4 next hop to a MAC address: the destination host for same-subnet delivery, or the default gateway for a remote destination. Hosts cache ARP mappings (arp -a). Switches separately learn source MAC-to-port mappings from Ethernet frames.

front: What does a broadcast packet look like?
back: Destination IP = all 255s (255.255.255.255); destination MAC = all Fs (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF).

front: TCP vs UDP — one-line each
back: TCP: connection-oriented, reliable, 3-way handshake (SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK), resends unacknowledged packets. UDP: connectionless, no ACKs, used for streaming/VoIP where speed beats reliability.

front: Total port count and the three port ranges
back: 65,536 TCP + 65,536 UDP = 131,072. Well-known 0-1023 (assigned protocols), registered (vendor apps, e.g. SQL 1433), high/dynamic (random client use).

front: QoS vs COS
back: Quality of Service on the LAN; Class of Service on the WAN — and only MPLS supported COS. Both prioritize voice/video traffic.

front: MPLS is legacy — what replaced it?
back: SD-WAN (software-defined WAN, configured on firewall/router, can still do QoS) or site-to-site VPNs over the internet. MPLS's unique feature was Class of Service.

front: Does Ethernet forwarding require every device to know every IP and MAC?
back: No. Switches learn source MAC-to-port mappings from frames. Hosts resolve the IPv4 next hops they need using ARP and cache those mappings. Routing convergence concerns agreement on usable routes; it does not require every host to know every address.

front: Workgroup vs domain — 2 traits each
back: Workgroup (peer-to-peer): not scalable, hard to manage, less secure, profile tied to one PC. Domain (client-server): scalable, manageable, secure, log in anywhere via the domain controller.

front: Network diagram symbols
back: Circle with X (or 4 criss-cross arrows) = router. Rectangle with one arrow = hub. Rectangle with two opposing arrows = switch.

front: PoE — what and why
back: Power over Ethernet: switch delivers low-voltage (<48V) power over the data cable; VoIP phones ship without power bricks. No PoE switch? Use a PoE injector.

front: How does a host choose the ARP target for local versus remote IPv4 delivery?
back: Compare the destination with the local subnet using the mask. Resolve the destination host locally; for a remote destination resolve the on-link default gateway. The packet keeps the remote destination IP.

front: Why did Lab 01’s wrong /24 mask break delivery from PC-A2 to Ops?
back: The approved plan uses /26. With /24, PC-A2 treated remote .74 as local and ARPed on Sales instead of using .1 as its gateway. Compare the mask with the plan and verify the repaired remote path.

front: What should be verified and documented after a next-hop repair?
back: Test relevant local, gateway and previously failed remote reachability. Record configuration, source/destination, tests and results. A successful ping supports tested IP reachability, not proof that every application works.

front: What does a router need to forward a packet?
back: The destination network, matched against its route table. It does not need the host, the origin network, or the return path.

front: Which addresses change at each routed hop, and which stay put (no NAT)?
back: MAC addresses are rebuilt at every hop. Source and destination IPs stay end to end; only TTL and the IPv4 checksum change.

front: Who does a host ARP for when the destination is remote?
back: The default gateway. The destination MAC is the gateway's, but the destination IP is unchanged.

front: How do you view the ARP cache on a host vs a Cisco router?
back: Host (Windows or Mac): arp -a. Cisco router or switch: show ip arp.

front: EtherType values to remember
back: 0x0800 = IPv4, 0x0806 = ARP. The FCS at the end of the frame is a 4-byte CRC that verifies the frame arrived intact.

front: What happens when a router has no matching route and no default route?
back: It drops the packet and sends an ICMP destination unreachable to the sender. The original packet is not returned.

front: Static vs dynamic routing in one line each
back: Static: an admin enters every route by hand and nothing updates itself. Dynamic: protocols share routes and tables update automatically.

front: What is an autonomous system, and which protocols go where?
back: A set of networks under one administrative domain. IGPs (RIP, EIGRP, OSPF) run inside it; the EGP (BGP) runs between autonomous systems.

front: In what order does a router pick among competing routes?
back: 1) Longest matching prefix, 2) lowest administrative distance, 3) lowest metric.

front: Typical administrative distances, lowest to highest
back: Connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120. Lower is more trusted.

front: What are the usable RIP hop counts?
back: 1 to 15. A hop count of 16 or more is unreachable.

front: RIPv2 update method?
back: Multicast to 224.0.0.9 every 30 seconds. It does not broadcast.

front: RIPv1 vs RIPv2: masks and authentication?
back: RIPv1 has neither. RIPv2 sends subnet masks and supports authentication.

front: Order the AD values
back: Connected 0, static 1, EIGRP internal 90, IGRP 100, OSPF 110, RIP 120, external EIGRP 170, unknown 255 (never used).

front: How does AD relate to metrics?
back: Lowest AD wins between sources. Metrics only break ties within the same protocol.

front: How is OSPF cost calculated?
back: Reference bandwidth (100 Mbps) divided by interface bandwidth. Faster links cost less.

front: What is EIGRP's metric?
back: A composite of delay, bandwidth, reliability, and load, weighted by K values.

front: Which protocols are link-state?
back: OSPF and IS-IS. They build the same topology map and run Dijkstra.

front: Does TTL expiry on its own mean there is a routing loop?
back: No. It can also mean the destination is too many hops away. A loop is packets circulating between routers and never arriving.

front: Static vs dynamic routing tradeoff?
back: Static stays until an admin changes it. Dynamic reroutes on failure but costs more RAM, CPU, and bandwidth.

front: What does a switch learn from, source or destination MAC?
back: The source MAC of incoming frames. The destination MAC decides where the frame is forwarded.

front: Unknown destination MAC arrives at a switch. What happens?
back: It floods the frame to all ports in the same VLAN only.

front: Hub vs bridge vs switch
back: Hub: multiport repeater, shared bandwidth. Bridge: software-based, slower. Switch: ASIC hardware, lowest latency.

front: Which VLANs are protected and cannot be deleted?
back: VLAN 1 and VLANs 1002 to 1005. All ports start in VLAN 1.

front: Access port vs trunk port
back: Access: one VLAN, tag removed before the frame leaves. Trunk: many VLANs, tags carried end to end.

front: Where does traffic go on a trunk with no tag?
back: The native VLAN. Tagged traffic is not placed there.

front: 802.1Q tag layout
back: 4 bytes between source MAC and type field: 16-bit TPID 0x8100, 3-bit CoS, 1-bit DEI, 12-bit VLAN ID.

front: STP root bridge and timing
back: Lowest priority wins (lowest MAC on a tie). Default port state is blocking; 50 seconds to forwarding.

front: Steps to segment R&D with flexibility
back: New VLAN, routed SVI, ACLs on the VLAN interface. Extended ACLs cannot go on layer 2 ports.

front: CoS vs ToS/DiffServ, PoE, VTP
back: CoS: layer 2, 3 bits in the tag, 8 queues. ToS/DiffServ: layer 3. 802.3at: 25.5 W. VTP propagates the VLAN database.

front: What do NDP and router advertisements do in IPv6?
back: NDP discovers neighboring devices. Router advertisements (RA) announce the gateway so hosts can find it.

front: Dual stack vs tunneling?
back: Dual stack runs IPv4 and IPv6 side by side. Tunneling carries IPv6 inside IPv4 (Teredo, ISATAP).

front: Internal vs external EIGRP AD?
back: Internal EIGRP 90. External EIGRP (routes redistributed into EIGRP) 170.

front: What does an AD of 255 mean?
back: The route source is unknown. The router never uses a route with AD 255.

front: Two updates list the same remote network. What does the router check first?
back: Administrative distance. The route with the lower AD is placed in the routing table.

front: What is the Class A first-octet range and default split?
back: 1 through 126, 8 network bits and 24 host bits.

front: What is the Class B first-octet range and default split?
back: 128 through 191, 16 network bits and 16 host bits.

front: What is the Class C first-octet range and default split?
back: 192 through 223, 24 network bits and 8 host bits.

front: What are the three RFC 1918 private ranges?
What does an address in 169.254.0.1 to 169.254.255.254 tell you?
back: APIPA: the client could not reach DHCP and configured itself, with mask 255.255.0.0.

front: Which class are Class D and Class E addresses?
back: D (224 to 239) is multicast. E (240 to 255) is experimental.

front: How long is an IPv6 address and how is it written?
back: 128 bits, written in hexadecimal. IPv4 is 32 bits in decimal.

front: Link-local vs unique local IPv6 addresses?
back: Both are non-Internet. Link-local is never routed. Unique local can be routed inside the organization.

front: Name three IPv6 compatibility methods.
back: Tunneling (IPv6 inside IPv4), dual stack (both side by side), and NAT64 (translate between IPv6 and IPv4).

front: How does EUI-64 build an IPv6 interface ID from a MAC address?
back: Insert FF:FE in the middle of the 48-bit MAC and invert the 7th bit of the first byte.

front: What defines a unicast address?
back: An address assigned to a single interface: one-to-one communication.

front: What defines a multicast address?
back: A one-to-many address, delivered to multiple interfaces.

front: What is an anycast address?
back: One address on multiple interfaces where the packet is delivered only to the first (nearest) one found: one-to-nearest.

front: What is the IPv6 loopback address?
back: ::1, the IPv6 version of 127.0.0.1.

front: What does an IPv6 link-local address always start with?
back: FE80::/10. It is not meant to be routed.

front: What does an IPv6 unique local address start with, and what is it like?
back: FC00::/7. Not routed to the Internet but still globally unique. Formerly called site-local.

front: Which IPv6 type is used like a regular public routable IPv4 address?
back: Global unicast.

front: What is the name for the 48-bit (6-byte) address physically assigned to a NIC?
back: A MAC address, also called a hardware address or burned-in address.

front: How many more bits does IPv6 have than IPv4?
back: 96 more: 128 bits compared with 32 bits.

front: What range counts as loopback in IPv4?
back: 127.0.0.1 through 127.255.255.254, used for loopback and diagnostics.

front: What are the default subnet masks for Class A, B, and C?
What are the big five subnetting questions?
back: How many subnets? How many hosts per subnet? What are the valid subnets? What is the broadcast address of each? What are the valid hosts?

front: How do you find the number of subnets?
back: 2 to the power of the subnet bits. One bit on in the interesting octet gives 2^1 = 2 subnets.

front: How do you find the hosts per subnet?
back: 2 to the power of the host bits, minus 2. A /25 has 7 host bits: 2^7 - 2 = 126.

front: Why do you subtract 2 from the host count?
back: One address is the subnet address (all host bits off) and one is the broadcast (all host bits on). Neither can be given to a host.

front: How do you find the block size?
back: 256 minus the mask value in the interesting octet. For 255.255.255.128: 256 - 128 = 128.

front: How do you find a subnet's broadcast address?
back: Take the number right before the next subnet. All host bits are on. For the 0 subnet in a /25, that is 127.

front: What are the valid hosts in a subnet?
back: Everything between the subnet address and the broadcast address.
2 subnets (0 and 128), 126 hosts each, broadcasts 127 and 255, hosts 1 to 126 and 129 to 254.

front: Class C /26 (255.255.255.192): block size, subnets, hosts?
back: Block size 64, 4 subnets, 62 hosts per subnet.

front: Class C /27 (255.255.255.224): block size, subnets, hosts?
back: Block size 32, 8 subnets, 30 hosts per subnet.

front: Which mask is best for a point-to-point WAN link, and why?
back: 255.255.255.252 (/30). It has 2 usable hosts, exactly the two ends of the link, and wastes nothing.

front: How many addresses does a /24 waste on a two-address WAN link?
back: 252 (254 hosts minus the 2 used).

front: What does CIDR notation tell you?
back: How many bits of the mask are on, written after a slash. 255.255.255.0 is /24.

front: What is a classful network versus classless routing?
back: Classful uses the same mask on every host and router interface. Classless lets different size masks be used (VLSM).

front: What is the difference between static NAT, dynamic NAT, and PAT?
back: Static: fixed one-to-one mapping. Dynamic: public addresses taken from a pool. PAT (NAT overloading): many hosts share one public address, separated by port numbers.

front: Which two names mean the same NAT feature?
back: NAT overloading and port address translation (PAT).

front: What is the network ID and host ID of 192.168.10.77 with mask 255.255.255.0?
back: Network ID 192.168.10 (the first three octets). Host ID 77 (the last octet).
